figures.title: Whole system overview
figures.caption: How do biology and context connect to cognitive function? This is an organising model, not one ADHD formula or a diagnostic graph.

sources.title: Demontis and colleagues rare variants 2026 issue

figures.long_description: Read from genes and regulation through development, precursor supply, cellular energy, synaptic communication and brain circuits to cognitive performance. Sleep, stress and environment are additional inputs. The connecting arrows organise relationships for learning; they do not demonstrate one causal chain, one defect shared by everybody with ADHD or a diagnostic test.

figures.title: Genes regulation and development
figures.caption: A genetic association and a molecular mechanism answer different questions. A pathway gene is not automatically an ADHD risk gene.
figures.long_description: DNA differences may influence regulation or protein sequence, but an associated locus, a candidate effector gene and a demonstrated mechanism are different levels of evidence. Developmental context can change the consequences. Common-variant and rare-variant ADHD studies support investigation of neuronal biology; they do not establish a shared defect in every patient or justify treating every pathway gene as an ADHD risk gene. The 2025 childhood GWAS has a publisher correction that should accompany use of that study.
figures.alt_text: Genes regulation and development. A genetic association and a molecular mechanism answer different questions.

figures.title: Amino acid supply and brain entry
figures.caption: Supply, transport and synthesis are separate control points. A blood level or dietary increase does not directly measure a synapse.
figures.long_description: Amino acids are supplied by diet and protein turnover. Brain entry is regulated by transporters, including LAT1, which transports several large neutral amino acids as part of an exchange system. Circulating abundance, transport competition, intracellular supply, enzyme activity and transmitter handling must be distinguished. More dietary precursor does not guarantee more transmitter released at a relevant synapse. The LAT1 experimental source includes mouse studies and human rare-variant observations, not a dietary ADHD treatment trial.

figures.title: Catecholamine synthesis and cell type branches
figures.caption: The catecholamine branch depends on which enzymes a cell expresses. Not every dopamine-producing neuron makes noradrenaline or adrenaline.
figures.long_description: Tyrosine hydroxylase forms L-DOPA in the cytosol; aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase forms dopamine. VMAT2 can transport dopamine into secretory vesicles. In cells expressing dopamine beta-hydroxylase, dopamine is converted to noradrenaline inside those vesicles, using copper and ascorbate. In cells expressing PNMT, noradrenaline returns to the cytosol for SAM-dependent conversion to adrenaline, which can be repackaged. These are cell-specific branches, not a compulsory chain in every dopamine neuron. Dopamine is the same molecule in peripheral and brain compartments.

figures.title: Vesicle loading and storage
figures.caption: ATP powers the vesicle's proton pump. VMAT2 uses the resulting proton gradient to load monoamines for storage and later release; it is not directly powered by ATP. This normal mechanism does not establish an individual transport defect.

sources.title: Transport and inhibition mechanism for VMAT2-mediated synaptic vesicle loading of monoamines — full text

figures.producer_caption: Why is cytosolic dopamine different from releasable dopamine? ATP powers the proton pump; do not draw VMAT2 as a direct ATP powered pump.
figures.long_description: ATP hydrolysis powers the vesicular proton pump, V-ATPase, which acidifies the vesicle. VMAT2 exchanges vesicular protons for cytosolic monoamines such as dopamine. It therefore uses an existing proton gradient rather than directly hydrolysing ATP itself. Stored transmitter can subsequently be released by exocytosis. This explains a normal mechanism, not evidence of a VMAT2 defect in a particular reader.
figures.alt_text: Vesicle loading and storage. ATP hydrolysis powers the vesicular proton pump, V-ATPase, which acidifies the vesicle.

figures.title: Release and vesicle recycling
figures.caption: Electrical activity, calcium entry and vesicle fusion are distinct steps. Vesicle membrane recycling is different from amino-acid recycling.
figures.long_description: At chemical synapses, action potentials and presynaptic calcium entry can trigger fusion of prepared vesicles. Calcium-sensing proteins and the SNARE machinery participate in release. Membrane retrieval and vesicle preparation permit reuse, but release and recycling comprise multiple processes rather than one invariant conveyor belt. Firing rate, vesicle loading, the size of the ready pool and release probability are separate controls. The diagram illustrates established synaptic physiology and does not locate an ADHD-specific release defect.
figures.alt_text: Release and vesicle recycling. Electrical activity, calcium entry and vesicle fusion are distinct steps.

figures.title: Synaptic clearance and intracellular metabolism
figures.caption: Transport out of the cleft and intracellular breakdown are different routes. MAO is not an enzyme floating freely in the synaptic cleft.
figures.long_description: Clearance from the extracellular space includes diffusion and transporter-mediated uptake. DAT is important in many dopamine regions; NET can also clear dopamine where DAT expression is low, including evidence from mouse prefrontal cortex. Intracellular dopamine can be re-stored or metabolised. MAO is associated with the outer mitochondrial membrane; its aldehyde products require further processing. COMT-dependent methylation is another route whose importance differs by cell and region. This concerns transmitter handling, not systemic metabolism of an ADHD medicine.

figures.caption: Receptor coupling is a starting point, not a complete prediction. A receptor family cannot be labelled universally good or bad for attention.
figures.long_description: The dopamine receptor nomenclature divides receptors into D1-like and D2-like families with different canonical G-protein coupling. figures.title: Energy supply and neuronal demand
figures.caption: Neurons use energy to maintain gradients and support signalling. This is normal physiology, not proof of an energy defect in ADHD.
figures.long_description: Aerobic metabolism supplies reducing equivalents to the respiratory chain. Proton pumping and ATP synthase couple electron transfer to ATP generation. Cells use ATP for ion homeostasis, biosynthesis and many aspects of signalling. Glycolysis also produces ATP, and fuel contributions differ with cell and context. Mitochondria do not directly manufacture dopamine. An explanation of energy supply and demand does not establish mitochondrial dysfunction or an energy deficit in an individual with ADHD.

figures.caption: Connectivity measures describe relationships in recorded brain activity. Dashed lines show statistical dependence, not axons or proven causal influence.

figures.title: BH4 synthesis and cofactor recycling
figures.caption: Making BH4, recycling it after hydroxylases and redox salvage are distinct. The hydroxylase cofactor cycle is not identical to NOS redox salvage.
figures.long_description: BH4 is made through GCH1, PTPS and SPR-dependent reactions and serves several enzymes. Aromatic-amino-acid hydroxylation generates a hydroxylated pterin intermediate; PCD and QDPR participate in regeneration. NOS has a different redox cycle, and oxidised BH2 can be reduced through DHFR-dependent salvage. These routes should not be collapsed into one chemical loop. Inherited biochemical disorders require their own clinical and laboratory assessment; ordinary ADHD does not by itself demonstrate such a disorder.
figures.alt_text: BH4 synthesis and cofactor recycling. Making BH4, recycling it after hydroxylases and redox salvage are distinct.

figures.title: Glutamate transmission
figures.caption: Glutamate transmission combines vesicle loading, receptors and uptake. An excitatory transmitter pathway is not a measure of ADHD severity.
figures.long_description: Presynaptic vesicular glutamate transporters load glutamate for release. Postsynaptic ionotropic and metabotropic receptors have different effects and kinetics. Extracellular glutamate is cleared by excitatory amino-acid transporters, including important astrocytic routes. Glutamine synthetase uses ATP to form glutamine, which can return to neurons. This is established neurotransmission; it does not diagnose excessive excitation, a glutamate defect or a particular cause of ADHD.

figures.title: GABA transmission and inhibition
figures.caption: GABA responses depend on receptor type and the ion gradient. GABA is usually inhibitory in mature contexts; that is not an absolute rule.
figures.long_description: GABA is produced from glutamate and released from vesicles. GABAA receptors conduct anions, so the effect depends on chloride/bicarbonate gradients and membrane potential, not just the name of the transmitter. GABAB receptors act through G proteins. Developmental induction of KCC2 contributes to more hyperpolarising GABAA responses in studied neurons. A depolarising response and net network excitation are also not automatically identical. The diagram makes no individual ADHD or developmental diagnosis.

figures.caption: Brain and peripheral serotonin are separate compartments. Serotonin is not simply a happiness chemical; tissue context matters.

figures.title: Acetylcholine and attention modulation
figures.caption: Acetylcholine is made, released, hydrolysed and its choline reused. DAT and MAO are not the main acetylcholine clearance pathway.
figures.long_description: Choline acetyltransferase synthesises acetylcholine from choline and acetyl-CoA. Vesicular transport and calcium-dependent exocytosis support release. Acetylcholinesterase, associated with extracellular membrane surfaces, rapidly hydrolyses the transmitter, and choline uptake supplies material for reuse. Nicotinic and muscarinic receptors act differently. Acetylcholine participates in many central and peripheral functions; a mechanism cartoon does not imply an attention-specific defect or justify an individual treatment.

figures.title: Redox balance and glutathione
figures.caption: Glutathione participates in redox chemistry; balance matters. This normal redox system does not establish oxidative stress as an ADHD cause.
figures.long_description: Glutathione synthesis combines glutamate and cysteine, then glycine, in ATP-requiring steps. Peroxidase reactions can oxidise reduced glutathione to GSSG while reducing peroxides. Glutathione reductase uses NADPH to regenerate GSH. Reactive species have normal signalling roles as well as damaging effects when regulation fails. The cycle is an educational simplification and not evidence that an individual has oxidative stress, requires an antioxidant or has ADHD because of a redox abnormality.

figures.caption: Circadian timing, sleep pressure and arousal interact but are not identical. Sleep loss can worsen performance without establishing the origin of ADHD.

figures.title: Mitochondrial membrane and respiratory chain
figures.caption: Electrons pass along the respiratory chain while complexes I, III and IV pump protons. Proton return through ATP synthase supports ATP formation. This illustrates general cell physiology; it does not establish an energy defect in a reader.
figures.producer_caption: Zoom further into the named parent process. Preserve compartment and reaction direction; check every added regulatory edge.
figures.long_description: NADH supplies electrons through complex I, while succinate oxidation supplies electrons through complex II. Ubiquinone transfers electrons to complex III, cytochrome c carries them to complex IV, and oxygen is the final acceptor. Complexes I, III and IV pump protons from the matrix towards the intermembrane space. Complex II is membrane-bound but does not pump protons; its label is placed on the matrix side in this simplified drawing. Proton return through ATP synthase supports ATP formation from ADP and phosphate. The diagram does not establish mitochondrial dysfunction in ADHD.

figures.title: BH4 hydroxylase recycling and salvage
figures.caption: Hydroxylase recycling and oxidised-BH2 salvage require different enzymes. Quinonoid BH2 and 7,8-BH2 must not be treated as one identical intermediate.
figures.long_description: Aromatic amino-acid hydroxylases form 4a-hydroxytetrahydrobiopterin. Pterin-4a-carbinolamine dehydratase produces quinonoid dihydrobiopterin, which QDPR can reduce using NADH to regenerate BH4. Oxidised 7,8-dihydrobiopterin belongs to a different salvage route using DHFR and NADPH. Non-enzymatic rearrangement and intermediate redox chemistry exist but are omitted here rather than drawn as an unverified universal arrow. This is an educational biochemical distinction, not proof of BH4 deficiency or an ADHD mechanism.

figures.title: Common locus to effector gene evidence
figures.caption: A genetic association identifies a region of interest. Connecting it to a candidate variant, gene and tissue-specific process requires several kinds of evidence. Each step has uncertainty; proximity alone does not establish causality.

figures.long_description: Begin with an associated locus, then evaluate fine-mapping, candidate variants, regulatory or coding consequences, potential effector genes and tissue-specific functions. Each step needs its own evidence. Linkage disequilibrium can leave several correlated candidates, and regulation may act over a distance. Proximity can be a clue but does not establish the causal gene by itself. These are complementary evidence types, not a mandatory sequence or a validated causal conclusion about one person.

figures.title: Amphetamine dexamfetamine at the dopamine terminal
figures.caption: Amphetamine mechanisms: experimental targets and clinical effects are distinct. A therapeutic dose or individual benefit cannot be read from this cartoon.
figures.long_description: Amphetamine acts as a substrate at monoamine transporters and can alter intracellular monoamine handling and support transporter-mediated efflux. Experimental work also identifies intracellular TAAR1 signalling and transporter trafficking. Vesicular stores affect availability, but knockout-culture evidence shows vesicular transport is not an absolute prerequisite for every experimental amphetamine action. Calcium-triggered exocytosis is therefore kept separate from efflux. Models, concentration and exposure conditions limit translation. The UK dexamfetamine SmPC does not claim a fully settled explanation of behavioural benefit in ADHD. No dose, efficacy, safety or individual mechanism is inferred.
